extracted.intended_audience: patentees, patent attorneys, and legal practitioners concerned with UK patent registration and infringement law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on registration/rectification of the patent register and substantive infringement doctrines: what amounts to infringement, scope of protection (principle vs form), mechanical equivalents, and the effect of registration and assignments on rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration withheld until patent sealed; deed stamping
rubrics_metrics.description: The registry refuses to register any document until the patent affected has been sealed. Deeds left for registration must be duly stamped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical requirement: do not present documents for registration before the patent is sealed; ensure deeds are properly stamped to be registrable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court power to rectify register (s.90)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court may, on application of any person aggrieved by omission without sufficient cause of a name or other particulars from the register, or by any entry made without sufficient cause, make such order for making, expunging, or varying the entry as the Court thinks fit, or may refuse the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court may also award costs, decide questions necessary for rectification, direct issues to be tried on questions of fact, and award damages to the party aggrieved. Any rectifying order must direct that due notice be given to the Comptroller; an office copy of the order must be left at the Patent Office (Patents Rules 1890, Rule 74).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rectification following foreign (Scotland/Ireland) court orders (s.111)
rubrics_metrics.description: If rectification of a register is required by any proceeding in a Court in Scotland or Ireland, a copy of the order, decree, or other authority for rectification must be served on the Comptroller, who is to rectify the register accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural duty to serve foreign-jurisdiction court instruments on the Comptroller so the central register can be amended to reflect those orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comptroller's power to correct clerical errors (s.91)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comptroller is empowered to correct any clerical error in the name, style, or address of the registered proprietor of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative remedy for obvious clerical mistakes without court application; limited to errors of form (name/style/address).

rubrics_metrics.name: False entries and forged copies are misdemeanours (s.98)
rubrics_metrics.description: The making of false entries in the register; the making of any writing falsely purporting to be a copy of an entry therein; and the tendering in evidence of any such writing, are declared to be severally misdemeanours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal sanction exists for fraudulent manipulation or falsification of the register or purported copies thereof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Former registers and public inspection (s.114 & Rule 79)
rubrics_metrics.description: Former registers of patents and proprietors are to be deemed parts of the register kept under the new Act, which is directed to be open at all convenient times to inspection of the public, subject to prescribed regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certified copies, sealed with the Patent Office seal, of any entry will be given to persons requiring same on payment of the prescribed fee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of non-registration of assignment on enforcement rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, until registration of an assignment the grantee was deemed the proprietor only after registration (1852 Act); an assignee could not always bring an action for infringement until assignment registered. However, courts have held in some cases an assignee may sue before registration where necessary (e.g., where the assignee has notice, or probate/assignment facts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration is important to protect enforcement rights, but equitable/practical exceptions exist; timing of registration can affect who may sue and whether registration relates back to assignment date (case law varies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration of an exclusive licence is not necessarily notice to the world
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration of an exclusive licence for a district is not in itself notice to the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration alone may not bind third parties as constructive notice of certain license rights; additional steps may be required to provide effective public notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court's role in register entries limited to facts, not legal inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the duty of the Court to insert on the register facts relating to proprietorship, but not the legal inferences to be drawn from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ordering changes, courts will record factual circumstances (e.g., existence and dates of deeds) rather than express conclusions about legal rights or priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of infringement (enumeration)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rights of a patentee may be violated in several ways: (1) the invention may be overtly exercised exactly as the specification has described it without permission; (2) the invention may be copied with changes/variations (additions, omissions, transpositions, substitutions) to produce something colourably different; (3) by dealing in articles made by the patented method without licence; (4) by the user of articles made by an infringement of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the principal paths by which infringement arises; the second (colourable imitation) gives most difficulty and requires careful analysis of substance vs form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance over form: look to the leading idea/principle
rubrics_metrics.description: When the leading idea or principle remains the same, contrivances will be considered identical; courts look to the substance and not merely the form of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where appearance differs, if the same principle is carried into effect or a substantial part of the patented property is taken, injunction and compensation may follow. Examples: cases where different constructions/forgings or material substitutions were nevertheless held to infringe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical equivalents doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: A person will not be allowed to deprive an inventor of the fruits of his discovery by substituting a well-known equivalent, either chemical or mechanical, for some part of the patented invention; courts will treat such substitutions as infringements where the principle/substance is the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to capture infringers who use equivalents to evade literal wording. Cases cited: Morgan v. Sycamore, Tinn v. Worthington, and many others. Apply when the equivalent carries out substantially the same function/principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colourable alterations and immaterial variations do not avoid infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: It will not be an infringement-avoiding strategy to disguise a patented invention by additions, subtractions, transpositions of parts, immaterial alterations of shape, or making a part act indirectly instead of directly, if the patented principle/substance is taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court authorities stress that if 'part of the property in the invention be really taken' there is an infringement regardless of disguises; examples include transpositions, shape alterations, and indirect action of parts (with case citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope when principle is new: broad protection for modes of carrying principle into effect
rubrics_metrics.description: When a mode of carrying a principle into effect has been invented and the principle itself is new, the patentee may secure not only that particular mode but every other mode of carrying the principle into effect (subject to nuance and limits in later authority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several judicial dicta support broad protection where the principle is new (Jupe v. Pratt; Houschill Co. v. Neilson); but later judges (e.g., L. J. Cotton) qualified this — courts look narrowly and examine whether differences are merely colourable. This doctrine is most applicable when the disclosed principle is genuinely novel and widely applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope when principle is not new: confined to the particular method described
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the principle is not new, the patentee is confined to the particular method described in the specification, and the patent will not be allowed to cover other methods; the doctrine of mechanical equivalents will not be applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts are 'more jealous' in such cases and will hold patentee to his described means. Examples: Curtis v. Platt; Bovill v. Pimm; Boyd v. Horrocks. If prior art shows the objective was known, the patentee cannot claim broadly to exclude all other means of achieving it.

rubrics_metrics.name: When patented machine/result is wholly novel, equivalents apply strongly
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the thing is wholly novel and the machine itself necessarily contains novelty in all its parts (and the result is new), courts look narrowly at alleged infringers and apply the doctrine of mechanical equivalents where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If both the combination and the result are new, a device producing the same result by substantially similar means will be treated as infringement (cases: Proctor v. Bennis; Gosnell v. Bishop; Ehrlich v. Ihlee).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interfering patents rule (priority and validity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever it appears that the use of a prior patent invention would be an infringement of a subsequent patent, the second (later) patent cannot be sustained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, a later patent that would require use of an earlier patented invention is invalid for lack of novelty/for interference with prior rights (authorities: Bush v. Fox and related cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent inventions producing same object may both be valid
rubrics_metrics.description: If two inventors independently devise different methods (distinct in substance) of achieving the same object, each may obtain protection for his own method; identity of object must not be mistaken for identity of means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bovill v. Pimm — two different ventilating solutions to the known problem of cooling grain were held independent and each inventor limited to the method described in his specification. Courts will allow different 'roads' to the same end when the means are truly distinct.
